nameStory: Smith's Longspur is named after Gideon B. Smith, a 19th-century American naturalist who collected specimens in the Arctic. The "longspur" part comes from the bird's elongated hind claw that extends backward like a tiny spur on a cowboy's boot.
description: Smith's Longspur is a sparrow-sized songbird that's built for life on the ground in open country. These chunky little birds are about the size of a House Sparrow, with streaky brown and buff plumage that helps them blend into grasslands and tundra. Males develop striking black and white head patterns during breeding season, while females and non-breeding birds show more subtle streaky brown coloring. They're ground-dwelling seed-eaters that hop and walk rather than perch high in trees.

idTips.label: Elongated hind claw
idTips.description: Look for the distinctively long, straight hind claw that extends well beyond the toe pad - you can often see this spur-like projection even from a distance

idTips.label: Ground-hugging behavior
idTips.description: Walks and hops on the ground with a distinctive crouched posture, rarely perching above knee height, often running between low cover

idTips.label: Breeding male head pattern
idTips.description: Males in spring show a bold black and white head with a bright white patch behind the eye that stands out like a headlight against the dark cap

idTips.label: Streaky back pattern
idTips.description: Rich brown and buff streaking on the back creates a complex pattern that looks almost woven, with each feather having multiple color bands

idTips.label: Chunky build
idTips.description: Noticeably stockier than most sparrows with a thick neck and robust body that gives them a sturdy, compact appearance

habitat: In New England, Smith's Longspurs are extremely rare visitors found only during migration in short-grass fields, airports, and coastal grasslands. They prefer areas with sparse, low vegetation where they can walk easily on the ground, such as recently mowed fields or areas with patchy grass coverage.

seasonality.spring: Very rare spring migrants may appear in April or May, with males showing their distinctive black and white breeding plumage.
seasonality.summer: Not present in New England during summer - they breed far north in Arctic Canada and Alaska.
seasonality.fall: Occasional fall migrants pass through in September or October, showing duller streaky plumage without the bold head patterns.
seasonality.winter: Extremely rare winter visitors, appearing as brown and buff streaky birds that blend well with dried grasses.

funFact: Smith's Longspurs have one of the most unusual migration routes of any North American bird - they breed in the far north but funnel through a narrow corridor in the Great Plains during migration, making them almost mythical for birdwatchers outside that pathway.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other longspurs, especially Lapland Longspur, but Smith's shows more buff and rust tones overall and lacks the Lapland's white wing patches in flight. The long hind claw is the sure-fire feature - if you can't see that distinctive spur, you might be looking at a regular sparrow.
contextualKnowledge: Smith's Longspurs are so rare in New England that any sighting becomes major birding news. Most of the 23 recorded observations likely represent single vagrant individuals that got blown off their normal migration route through the central United States.
compareHints: Compared to the more common Lapland Longspur, Smith's Longspur shows warmer buff and rust tones rather than black and white contrasts, and lacks the white wing patches visible in flight. Smith's also has a more upright posture when walking and tends to be found in shorter grass habitats.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Lapland longspur is the only member of its genus regularly seen in New England, making it unique among the typical longspurs.

Compared to the more likely Lapland longspur, chestnut-collared longspurs are smaller and more compact, with that distinctive chestnut collar in breeding males versus the Lapland's black throat and face markings.
